kicker: GTA V in a browser tab

scenes.headline: How GTA V runs inside a browser tab
scenes.sub: The real engine, recompiled to WebAssembly and WebGPU
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Samosa! Grand Theft Auto Five now runs in Chrome. Not streamed, not emulated. Here is how.

scenes.text: The game's own engine is compiled to 64-bit WebAssembly, and its threads reach the browser only through shared memory.
scenes.say: The idea: compile the game's own engine to sixty-four bit WebAssembly, and let its threads reach the browser only through shared memory.

steps.say: The engine runs as real threads that block and wait.
They never call the browser. They write requests into shared memory.
The page drops keys in there too.
Small workers pick them up: graphics, files, sound.

items.say: The engine still talks to Direct3D eleven, but the device is a fake.
Each call becomes a small command in a ring buffer.
A worker that owns the WebGPU device replays them in order.
Every shader was translated ahead of time. Geometry and tessellation shaders have no WebGPU stage, so they are dropped.

scenes.title: A file system made of requests

steps.say: When the engine reads a file, it fills a slot in memory and waits.
A worker checks a block store in the browser's private file system.
Missing blocks come from the server, many requests at once.
The bytes land in the engine's heap, and the thread wakes.

scenes.label: of game archives, fetched only as the world needs them
scenes.say: That is how about twenty-one gigabytes of game data can sit behind a tab. Only the blocks the world needs are ever fetched.

steps.say: I ran it on a server with no graphics card. Chrome drew it in software, slowly, but this is the real world.
Same engine, same data, inside a browser tab.

scenes.text: Shared memory and atomics let blocking C++ threads live beside a browser that only speaks async.
scenes.say: The lesson: shared memory and atomics let blocking engine threads live beside a browser that only speaks async.

recap: Files streamed in blocks on demand
scenes.say: The real engine, Direct3D replayed on WebGPU, and files streamed in blocks.
